messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Malik, a 22‑year‑old South‑Eastern Asian university student, returned home from a month’s relief work in a war‑torn district of Syria. He had been assigned to a makeshift clinic on the outskirts of a besieged town, where the constant artillery chatter and the sight of men in dark field‑issued uniforms filled his days. One afternoon, while transporting a stretcher, a burst of gunfire erupted just meters away; the nearest soldier’s eyes seemed to lock on him, as if the very act of moving a wounded child made him the focus of a predator’s gaze. The memory of that instant— the feel of the gunshot shuddering through his body, the oppressive weight of the uniforms surrounding him, the sharp scent of cordite—has remained lodged in Malik’s mind like a live wire. From that day on, he reports a pervasive sense of being watched, a constant fear that authority figures—police or military—might appear at any moment and scrutinize him. Those triggers immediately translated into concrete avoidance behaviours. Malik began refusing to attend the weekly student association meetings, citing a need to stay off the “camera” of anyone he had known before the war. When classmates greeted him at the campus café, he would avert his gaze, leaving his eyes fixed on the floor or the coffee mug, avoiding the inevitable, “I need to keep from looking directly at people.” A week later, he told his roommate that he could not stand in the campus security office during exams, citing the dread of seeing uniformed officers, and when the university announced a field‑trip to a nearby historical site—where uniforms would be mandatory—he quietly dropped out of the itinerary. These maladaptive strategies were, in Malik’s mind, rational responses to a world that still felt, in parts, hostile and surveilled. The same triggers also triggered a set of harsh, self‑critical beliefs. Each time he caught himself avoiding eye contact or withdrawing from a social interaction, Malik would immediately blame his own failure: “I am the only one who didn’t keep the peace,” he told himself, believing that his perceived lack of courage had betrayed his role as a humanitarian. The memory of his body trembling with adrenaline during the firefight—he described it as if his body had become an enemy, a weapon against his own safety—reinforced the notion that his physical responses were a sign of impending danger, even in the quiet halls of the university library. Furthermore, Malik’s sense of helplessness grew: every time he was told to stay in the classroom or to answer a question, he felt the old image of the enemy’s silhouette flash in his mind, and the belief that “bad things will happen to me again” seemed inevitable. This negative appraisal loop was not just a reaction to triggers; it fed back into them. The more Malik felt powerless, the more he interpreted everyday authority—such as a professor’s raised voice or a campus security officer’s badge—as a threat, thereby reinforcing the sense that he was being watched. The avoidance behaviours, in turn, had tangible consequences. Malik’s declining attendance left him missing critical lab reports, and the isolation he cultivated made it difficult for him to collaborate on group projects. His friends, once eager to discuss his overseas experiences, gradually stopped reaching out, assuming he was simply preoccupied with studies. Malik’s grades slipped, and a conversation with his academic advisor prompted him to consider withdrawing from the program altogether. The anxiety that had started in the war zone now seeped into his academic life, eroding the very identity he once claimed to have defended. In a conversation with a peer, Malik confessed, “I keep thinking they’re looking at me, even when I’m alone in the dorm, and I can’t even sit in the lecture hall without feeling like everyone’s watching.” Today, Malik sits in a therapist’s office for the first time, his voice shaking as he recounts how the weight of that memory has grown. His PCL‑5 score of 78 indicates severe symptomatology. He says he has reached a breaking point: the persistent feeling that his body is a weapon of danger, the belief that he has failed in his most important role, and the helplessness that everything seems to be out of his control. Malik is most afraid that he will never feel safe enough to speak in front of his classmates again, and he hopes that through therapy he can regain the ability to trust his own body and to see authority figures as neutral, rather than menacing.
